The FOMC’s decision to hold the federal funds rate at 5.25–5.50 percent and continue balance-sheet runoff is consistent with rules- and forecast-based frameworks (Clarida–Galí–Gertler; Svensson–Woodford), the New Keynesian emphasis on inflation expectations, and time-inconsistency lessons that argue for patience until inflation is sustainably near 2 percent. Recent data show solid activity, easing but still-elevated inflation, and risks moving into better balance—supporting a cautious hold.

Incorporating the Federal Reserve’s Financial Stability Report, however, tempers the tone: the FSR highlights ongoing vulnerabilities—elevated valuation pressures, persistent interest rate volatility, structural funding risks in money market funds and other nonbank intermediation, leveraged hedge fund activity in Treasury markets, commercial real estate stress (notably office vacancy rates), sizable public debt and term-premium sensitivity, and global risks (including China and geopolitics). At the same time, the FSR notes the U.S. financial system’s resilience, with bank capital and liquidity still solid. Together, these points reinforce staying restrictive and continuing QT while avoiding an overly upbeat assessment.

Netting these factors yields a mildly positive but more guarded stance than before. sentiment score = 0.30
